claims.text: Single-source precursors reduced at low or moderate temperature can form multi-element HEA nanoparticles.
Reduction of solid, mixed single-source precursors at low or moderate temperature limits free atomic mobility.
Increasing the number of element types under limited-mobility conditions increases the likelihood of forming a random, single-phase alloy.
Limited atomic mobility opposes structural preferences arising from differences in elemental interactions or mixing enthalpies during particle formation.
The synthesized HEA nanoparticles are near-equiatomic.
Limited mobility anchors the constituent elements into a single-phase lattice.
A kinetically frozen random alloy produced during synthesis remains resistant to elemental segregation and phase separation during later high-temperature service.
This high-temperature stabilization persists over catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
The proposed high-temperature stabilization applies even when noble-metal content is low.
A post-synthesis anneal at a moderately elevated temperature below the service regime increases atomic mobility relative to the unannealed baseline.
Anneal-enhanced mobility permits atomic rearrangement and increases local elemental segregation.
Anneal-enhanced mobility promotes formation of secondary phases during subsequent service exposure.
Unannealed, mobility-restricted nanoparticles will retain a uniform elemental distribution and single-phase structure after high-temperature exposure.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit more elemental segregation than the unannealed baseline.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit increased lattice strain relative to the unannealed baseline.
Segregation and secondary-phase formation will reduce catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to solution-based syntheses because atomic mobility is inherently higher there.
The mobility thresholds and thermal budgets that trigger segregation are not defined.
Support interactions and surface effects are not controlled or mechanistically resolved.
Comparable segregation, phase separation, or performance degradation in annealed and unannealed samples is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: A below-service-temperature anneal is said to restore enough mobility to induce segregation, while much hotter subsequent service temperatures—up to 1923 K—are said not to overcome the synthesis-imposed mobility restriction in the baseline. The hypothesis does not explain why mobility activated during the lower-temperature anneal would remain suppressed during hotter service.
